root_cause_pattern: Missing or inadequate type annotations and imports in Python code — static type checkers fail when typing constructs (Any, Dict, Union) are used without proper imports, or when runtime values from dicts are used without type validation.
cascade_pattern: Static analysis tools (ruff, mypy) detect undefined typing names or unsafe type operations and fail the CI pipeline. These failures cascade from the immediate lint/type check step to block any downstream CI stages.
principle: error_type=Type Checking: Always explicitly import typing constructs (Any, Dict, Union, etc.) before using them in type annotations, and validate the types of values retrieved from dictionaries before performing operations on them. Static type checkers enforce strict rules that require both proper imports and runtime type safety.
fix_strategy: 1. Audit all files for typing constructs used in annotations and ensure proper imports from typing module. 2. Add isinstance or type checks before operating on values retrieved from dictionaries. 3. Run type checkers (ruff, mypy) to verify all type-related errors are resolved before CI submission.
fix_strategies: 1. Audit all files for typing constructs used in annotations and ensure proper imports from typing module. 2. Add isinstance or type checks before operating on values retrieved from dictionaries. 3. Run type checkers (ruff, mypy) to verify all type-related errors are resolved before CI submission.
failure_reasons: Using typing constructs without importing them from the typing module causes undefined name errors in static analysis
Retrieving values from dictionaries and using them without type validation causes type safety violations in static analysis

root_cause_pattern: A third-party library underwent a breaking API change — its public exports were reorganized (classes moved to submodules) and methods were renamed, causing import failures in consumer code that references the old import paths and method names.
cascade_pattern: When a library reorganizes its exports or renames methods, the import statements in dependent code become invalid. This causes ImportError during module loading, which blocks test collection and prevents any downstream tests from running. Additionally, method calls using old names fail at runtime.
principle: error_type=Dependency Error: Always verify that your import paths and method calls match the current API of your dependencies. Library maintainers may move exports to different submodules or rename methods without backward compatibility — pin dependency versions and audit imports when upgrading. When import errors occur, check if the library has reorganized its module structure or renamed its public API.
fix_strategy: 1. Identify the correct new import path for the relocated class (check library's __init__.py or types submodule). 2. Update all import statements to use the new module path. 3. Scan for renamed methods/functions and update all call sites. 4. Consider pinning dependency versions in requirements to prevent unexpected breaking changes.

root_cause_pattern: CI failures stem from code that depends on assumptions which can change — either internal assumptions about attribute initialization or external assumptions about third-party package APIs. When these assumptions are violated (due to refactoring or upstream library updates), static analysis and import resolution fail.
cascade_pattern: When the root assumption violation occurs, the immediate CI tool (mypy or pytest) fails during its check phase. For type checking, mypy exits with attr-defined errors. For imports, pytest fails during test collection because the module cannot be loaded. These failures block downstream CI jobs since they prevent the pipeline from reaching execution.
principle: Always write defensive code that handles both internal attribute lifecycle and external dependency API variability. For attributes, define them before use in __init__. For imports, use conditional imports or try/except chains to support multiple API versions of third-party packages. This ensures CI tooling can successfully analyze and load your code regardless of upstream changes.
fix_strategy: 1. Identify all attribute references in __init__ methods and ensure each is defined before first use with proper type annotations. 2. For third-party imports, implement try/except import chains to support legacy and current API versions. 3. Use alias patterns to normalize different API versions to a single internal name. 4. Update test mocks to use method-level spec rather than importing concrete classes when those classes have unstable APIs. 5. Run type checking and test collection to verify fixes.

root_cause_pattern: Type annotations declare one type (e.g., str return type or Union[str, PathLike[str]] parameter) while actual runtime values are of a different, incompatible type (e.g., RunResponse object or Optional[Any]). The mismatch occurs because code returns objects or passes values without ensuring type compatibility with declared annotations.
cascade_pattern: When mypy runs in strict mode, it performs comprehensive type inference and validation. Any function returning a type incompatible with its annotation, or any function receiving a nullable value where a non-null type is expected, causes immediate type-checking failure. These are independent type errors that each cause the CI pipeline to fail the build.
principle: Always align runtime values with declared type annotations. When a function declares a return type, the actual return value must be that exact type—if conversion is needed, explicitly convert. When passing values to functions expecting non-null types, use type guards (conditional checks) to ensure the value is not None before passing it. Strict type checking will catch any mismatches, so ensure type compatibility at the source.
fix_strategy: 1. Identify the declared return type or parameter type from the type annotation. 2. Verify the actual runtime value type being returned or passed. 3. For return type mismatches: wrap the return value with appropriate type conversion (e.g., str()) to match declared type. 4. For nullable argument errors: add a conditional type guard (if value is not None) before passing to the function. 5. Re-run the type checker to verify all type errors are resolved.

Run type checkers to verify signature compatibility. 6. Consider pinning dependency versions to prevent unexpected API breaks.

cascade_pattern: When a formatting check fails early in CI and uses strict abort behavior, the workflow terminates before dependency validation and test execution stages can run. This prevents import errors and test assertion failures from being discovered, forcing multiple CI iteration cycles to surface all issues.
principle: CI pipelines should be designed to surface ALL failures in a single run rather than aborting on the first error. Use non-aborting modes for early-stage checks (formatting, linting) or run them as separate parallel jobs so that downstream failures (dependency errors, test failures) are also reported. This prevents wasted CI cycles and ensures developers see the complete picture of what needs fixing.

Ensure dependency checks and test execution stages run regardless of formatting results. 3. root_cause_pattern: Using conditional imports (try/except blocks) for optional dependencies without defining explicit type fallbacks causes the type checker to infer overly permissive Optional or generic types. These inferred types then propagate through the codebase whenever the conditional import fails.
cascade_pattern: When an optional dependency import fails at runtime, mypy infers a broader type (e.g., Optional[dict[str, Any]]) from the except branch. This flows downstream into functions expecting more specific types. Type mismatches manifest far from the original import site, making debugging difficult. The inferred Optional types also affect mock objects in tests, creating additional type chain violations.
principle: Always provide explicit type guards or type aliases when using conditional imports for optional dependencies. Rather than relying on the type checker to infer fallback types from except branches, define concrete type fallbacks and use helper methods or type guards to ensure consistent, specific types propagate through your codebase. This prevents cascading type errors that originate from lenient type inference at import boundaries.
fix_strategy: 1. Identify conditional import patterns (try/except) for optional dependencies. 2. Define explicit type fallbacks or type aliases for each conditional import. 3. Add type guard methods to validate and narrow the imported types before use. 4. Initialize nullable variables with default values before passing them to functions expecting non-optional types. 5. Remove unnecessary imports that create unwanted type dependencies in test files. 6. Run type checker to verify type consistency throughout the call chain.

root_cause_pattern: Optional dependencies are imported at module load time with hard ImportError raises, causing pytest's test collection phase to fail with exit code 2 before any tests can execute.
cascade_pattern: When pytest performs --collect-only, it imports all test modules and their dependencies. A hard ImportError in any imported file during collection causes the entire pytest run to abort immediately, preventing any test execution regardless of whether those failing imports are relevant to the test suite.
principle: Optional dependencies must be deferred to runtime — never raise ImportError at import time. Use try/except to import optional modules, set classes to None on failure, and add runtime checks before usage. This allows test collection to succeed even when optional dependencies are missing.
fix_strategy: 1. Replace hard ImportError raises in except blocks with setting imported classes to None. 2. Add try/except blocks with fallback aliases for renamed/moved classes. 3. Add runtime checks (if class is None) before using optional functionality. 4. Verify pytest --collect-only passes after fixes.

Add runtime checks (if class is None) before using optional functionality. 4. Verify pytest --collect-only passes after fixes.

root_cause_pattern: Variables initialized with empty collection literals without explicit type annotations cause the type checker to infer overly broad types that are incompatible with subsequent nullable assignments or usage patterns.
cascade_pattern: Type checker infers incorrect types from unannotated empty collections; when the variable is later assigned a nullable value or used in a context expecting a narrower type, the mismatch triggers type errors that fail the CI job.
principle: Always annotate variables that may hold nullable values with explicit type hints, especially when initializing with empty collections. An empty dict `{}` or list `[]` without annotation infers as the broadest possible type, making later nullable assignments incompatible. Use explicit `None` initialization combined with type annotations, and employ null guards and type narrowing checks before dereferencing nullable values.
fix_strategy: 1. Add explicit type annotations to all variables initialized with empty collections. 2. When a variable may hold nullable values, initialize with `None` and use a compatible type annotation. 3. Add null checks (e.g., `if value is not None:`) before using nullable values. 4. Use isinstance checks or type narrowing after null guards to refine types for downstream operations.

Use isinstance checks or type narrowing after null guards to refine types for downstream operations.

root_cause_pattern: Code references names (functions, classes, constants) from other modules without those names being imported into the current module's namespace. This occurs when developers add new code that uses external symbols but fail to add the corresponding import statements.
cascade_pattern: The linter immediately detects the undefined names and fails the CI check. There is no downstream cascade because the linter catches the error at the source file where the undefined names are used.
principle: When adding code that uses symbols from other modules, always verify that those symbols are properly imported into the module's namespace before the code is committed. The import must appear before the symbol is referenced. This is a fundamental Python requirement — undefined names cannot be resolved at runtime or lint time without proper imports.

Add the appropriate import statement to the file, ensuring it appears before the name is used. 4. Re-run the linter to confirm all undefined name errors are resolved.

cascade_pattern: When a third-party package renames classes or lacks type stubs, the importing code fails at import time during pytest collection, and mypy fails when type annotations don't match actual behavior or stub packages are missing, blocking CI validation.
principle: Always implement defensive dependency handling: use conditional imports with fallbacks for version-sensitive third-party APIs, and ensure type annotations match actual return types while including stub packages for optional dependencies. Add fallback imports for renamed classes (e.g., try original name, then renamed name as alias). 3. Ensure type annotations match actual return types (use Union types for polymorphic returns). 4. Add isinstance checks before passing nullable values to functions expecting non-null types. 5. Include stub package entries in pyproject.toml for optional dependencies to satisfy mypy.

root_cause_pattern: Developers write code that violates project-specific style and type-checking rules (line length limits, whitespace conventions, no duplicate definitions) without running the same CI tooling locally, causing failures when the CI pipeline enforces these standards.
cascade_pattern: When CI runs linters and type checkers, they detect violations that were invisible during local development. These failures block merge, forcing fixes after code is 'complete' rather than catching issues early in the development cycle.
principle: Always run the same linting and type-checking tools locally that your CI pipeline uses, ideally via pre-commit hooks. Code that passes locally but fails in CI indicates a tooling gap between development and CI environments — not a CI problem.
fix_strategy: 1. Identify which tools run in CI (ruff, mypy, etc.). 2. Configure those same tools locally with identical settings. 3. Set up pre-commit hooks to run these tools before each commit. 4. Fix any violations the tools report. 5. Verify CI passes after fixes.

root_cause_pattern: A function declares a non-None return type annotation but contains a bare `return` statement (returning nothing/None) in at least one code path, creating a type contract violation where the actual return behavior does not match the annotated return type.
cascade_pattern: When the type checker (mypy) analyzes the function, it detects the mismatch between the annotated return type and the bare return statement, flagging a 'Return value expected' error. This causes the type checking CI step to fail, blocking the build.
principle: In Python, a bare `return` statement implicitly returns None, which is NOT compatible with non-None type annotations. When you declare a return type annotation (e.g., `-> dict`), you are contractually obligated to return a value of that type on ALL code paths. A bare `return` violates this contract. Always ensure your return statements explicitly return a value compatible with your type annotation, or update the annotation to include None (e.g., `-> Optional[dict]`).

Determine the appropriate fix: either provide the expected return value, change `return` to `return None` if None is valid, or update the return type to Optional/Union to include None. 3. Run the type checker (mypy) to verify the fix resolves all type errors.

Add explicit None checks (if var is not None:) or assertions (assert var is not None) before each access. 4. Use early returns or conditional logic to narrow types in all code paths. 5. Run mypy locally to verify all type narrowing is sufficient before pushing.

root_cause_pattern: Using Python version-specific type annotation syntax (such as the X | Y union syntax introduced in Python 3.10) in a codebase that targets an older Python version, combined with unsafe attribute access on union types through isinstance checks that mypy cannot properly narrow.
cascade_pattern: When mypy runs, it detects type incompatibilities: the union syntax is flagged as invalid for the target Python version, and isinstance checks accessing attributes exclusive to one union member produce type errors. These errors block the CI pipeline at the type-checking stage, preventing any downstream validation.
principle: Always ensure type annotations use syntax compatible with the project's minimum Python version target. For Python < 3.10, use Union[X, Y] from the typing module rather than the X | Y syntax. When working with union types, avoid isinstance checks that access attributes present only on specific union members—instead refactor to use explicit type narrowing, separate handlers for each type, or accept a single type to simplify the interface.

Remove isinstance checks that access union-member-specific attributes; either narrow the type explicitly or create separate code paths for each union member. 4. Run mypy to verify all type errors are resolved.

Run mypy to verify all type errors are resolved.

root_cause_pattern: Tests assert exact string equality against values that the implementation returns in a different format (e.g., full paths vs. basenames, or strings with additional context). The test expectations do not match the actual return format of the code under test.
cascade_pattern: When test assertions use exact equality (==) but the implementation returns strings with additional content (paths, prefixes, suffixes), the assertions fail immediately, causing the test suite to fail and blocking CI pipelines.

root_cause_pattern: Tests contain mock assertions that verify internal implementation details (specific function calls with exact arguments) rather than functional outcomes. This creates brittle tests that are tightly coupled to internal code structure.
cascade_pattern: When internal implementation changes—even correctly—the mock assertions fail because they check exact call patterns. The pytest -x flag stops at the first failure, causing the entire CI pipeline to fail despite the actual functionality working correctly.
principle: Tests should verify WHAT the code does (behavior and outcomes), not HOW it does it (internal function calls). Mock assertions that check specific internal call patterns with exact arguments create fragile tests that break during legitimate refactoring. Always test functional outcomes rather than implementation details.
fix_strategy: 1. Identify mock verification assertions that check internal call patterns (e.g., assert_called_once_with specific arguments). 2. Remove these brittle assertions. 3. Replace with functional assertions that verify the actual behavior or return values. 4. Ensure tests validate outcomes, not implementation details.
fix_strategies: 1. Identify mock verification assertions that check internal call patterns (e.g., assert_called_once_with specific arguments). 2. Remove these brittle assertions. 3. Replace with functional assertions that verify the actual behavior or return values. 4. Ensure tests validate outcomes, not implementation details.
failure_reasons: Tests verify internal implementation details through mock assertions rather than testing functional outcomes
Mock assertions couple tests to specific internal function calls and exact arguments, making them fragile to code changes

root_cause_pattern: The root cause is mismatched type documentation between docstrings and actual implementation (declaring non-optional return types when None is possible) and incorrect use of identity comparison operator (`is`) instead of equality operator (`==`) for constant literals.
cascade_pattern: When the linter runs, it detects type mismatches and incorrect comparison operators, exiting with a non-zero code. This causes the CI linting job to fail, blocking the pipeline.
principle: Always ensure docstring return types accurately reflect what the implementation can return, including None/Optional cases. Never use the identity operator (`is`) to compare constant literals like strings, bytes, or integers—always use equality (`==`) instead. Run linters locally before committing to catch these static analysis violations.
fix_strategy: 1. Audit docstrings for methods that may return None and update return types to Optional[T] or include None in documentation. 2. Replace all `is` comparisons with `==` when comparing against constant literals. 3. Run the linter locally (e.g., `ruff check`) before pushing code to catch formatting issues.
fix_strategies: 1. Audit docstrings for methods that may return None and update return types to Optional[T] or include None in documentation. 2. Replace all `is` comparisons with `==` when comparing against constant literals. 3. Run the linter locally (e.g., `ruff check`) before pushing code to catch formatting issues.
failure_reasons: Docstring declared non-optional return type but implementation can return None
Code used identity operator (`is`) instead of equality operator (`==`) for comparing constant bytes/string literals

root_cause_pattern: When a function or attribute is relocated to a different module during refactoring, any import statements that still reference the old module path will fail because the attribute no longer exists at that location.
cascade_pattern: The type checker (mypy) performs static analysis on imports before code execution, so it immediately fails when it cannot resolve an imported attribute to its definition. This prevents the CI pipeline from passing regardless of whether the code would actually run.
principle: Always update import statements when moving code between modules. Type checkers validate import resolution at static analysis time, so stale imports referencing old module paths will always be caught by CI tooling. Maintain a consistent mapping between where code lives and where it is imported from.
fix_strategy: 1. Identify all files importing the relocated attribute from the old module path. 2. Update each import statement to reference the new module location where the attribute is now defined. 3. Run the type checker to verify all imports are resolved correctly. 4. Search the codebase for any remaining references to the old import path to ensure completeness.
fix_strategies: 1. Identify all files importing the relocated attribute from the old module path. 2. Update each import statement to reference the new module location where the attribute is now defined. 3. Run the type checker to verify all imports are resolved correctly. 4. Search the codebase for any remaining references to the old import path to ensure completeness.
failure_reasons: Code was moved to a new module but import statements were not updated to reflect the new location
Type checker detected an imported attribute that does not exist at the specified module path

root_cause_pattern: Inadvertent trailing whitespace introduced in source code (e.g., extra spaces at end of lines in docstrings or comments) that violates strict formatting rules enforced by automated formatters like Black.
cascade_pattern: The formatter runs in CI as a gating check, detects the trailing whitespace violation, reports the file needs reformatting, and fails the build with a non-zero exit code, blocking all downstream jobs and preventing merge.
principle: Automated code formatters enforce strict whitespace rules and will reject code with even minor violations like trailing spaces. Developers must configure their editors and workflows to automatically strip trailing whitespace on save and run formatters locally before committing. Implementing pre-commit hooks that run the same formatter used in CI catches these issues before they reach the repository.
fix_strategy: 1. Identify the exact line(s) containing trailing whitespace using the formatter's output. 2. Remove all trailing whitespace from those lines (editor find/replace or automated tool). 3. Run the formatter locally (e.g., black .) to verify compliance. 4. Commit the cleaned changes. 5. Configure editor/IDE to strip trailing whitespace on save and add pre-commit hooks for future prevention.

Remove all trailing whitespace from those lines (editor find/replace or automated tool). 3. Run the formatter locally (e.g., black .) to verify compliance. 4. Commit the cleaned changes. 5. Configure editor/IDE to strip trailing whitespace on save and add pre-commit hooks for future prevention.
failure_reasons: Extra trailing whitespace characters at end of a line in a docstring that do not conform to Black's strict formatting requirements
Local development environment not configured to strip or warn about trailing whitespace, allowing non-conforming code to be committed

error_type: Multi-failure CI misattribution with type-checking error
root_cause_pattern: When multiple CI tools fail simultaneously (e.g., pytest and mypy), developers may incorrectly associate unrelated file modifications with CI failures, while the actual type-checking errors go unaddressed due to misattribution.
cascade_pattern: A multi-tool CI run produces separate failures (test collection error + type-checking error), but without careful diagnosis, the wrong file gets flagged as problematic. The cosmetic changes to one file distract from fixing the actual type annotation error in a different file.
principle: In CI pipelines running multiple validation tools (pytest, mypy, etc.), each failure must be traced independently to its source file. Cosmetic or documentation changes in a commit are not the root cause of type-checking failures — the actual type annotation error in the failing file must be fixed. Never assume a modified file is responsible for a CI failure without verifying which tool actually failed on which file.
fix_strategy: 1. Run each failing CI tool independently to isolate failures. 2. For each tool failure, identify the exact file and line number reported. 3. Verify the reported file actually contains the problematic code, not just any modified file. 4. Fix the type annotation or code causing the tool-specific error. 5. Confirm the fix resolves the specific CI tool failure, not just any failure in the pipeline.
fix_strategies: 1. Run each failing CI tool independently to isolate failures. 2. For each tool failure, identify the exact file and line number reported. 3. Verify the reported file actually contains the problematic code, not just any modified file. 4. Fix the type annotation or code causing the tool-specific error. 5. Confirm the fix resolves the specific CI tool failure, not just any failure in the pipeline.
failure_reasons: Multiple CI tools failing in one run leads to misattribution of root cause to unrelated file changes
Type annotation violates mypy strict type-checking rules causing CI type-checking job to fail

root_cause_pattern: A subclass provides concrete method implementations that do not properly match the abstract interface defined in the base class, causing the type checker to consider the class non-instantiable because the abstract method contract is not satisfied.
cascade_pattern: When a class fails to properly implement an abstract interface, the type checker flags it as non-instantiable. This type error propagates through CI, blocking the build because the type checker (mypy) enforces strict abstract class contracts.
principle: When extending abstract base classes in Python, method signatures must exactly match the abstract interface—including parameter types and return types. If you do not need to implement a method, do not override it; if you do override it, the signature must be identical to the abstract definition. Type checkers enforce these contracts strictly and will reject classes that appear to violate the abstract interface.
fix_strategy: 1. Review the abstract base class to understand the exact method signatures required. 2. Remove or fix method implementations that don't match the abstract interface exactly. 3. Ensure all method signatures (parameters, return types) conform precisely to the abstract definition. 4. Run type checker to verify the class is now properly instantiable.
fix_strategies: 1. Review the abstract base class to understand the exact method signatures required. 2. Remove or fix method implementations that don't match the abstract interface exactly. 3. Ensure all method signatures (parameters, return types) conform precisely to the abstract definition. 4. Run type checker to verify the class is now properly instantiable.
failure_reasons: A subclass provides method implementations that do not conform to the abstract interface contract
Type checking fails because the class is considered non-instantiable due to abstract method violations

root_cause_pattern: Developers added imports without verifying they were actually used in the code, and/or placed import statements after other executable code (like variable assignments) instead of at the module level, violating Python import placement conventions that linters enforce.
cascade_pattern: The linter (ruff) scans the codebase and flags violations as errors. When violations are found, the CI pipeline fails at the pre-merge check stage, blocking the code change from being merged until the formatting issues are resolved.
principle: Always place all module-level imports at the very top of the file, before any other statements. Only import symbols that are actually referenced in the code. Unused imports create dead code and violate linter rules; misplaced imports violate Python style conventions enforced by modern linters.
fix_strategy: 1. Run the linter to identify all import-related violations. 2. Remove any unused imports (imports present but not referenced in the file). 3. Move any imports that appear after executable code to the top of the file, before all other statements. 4. Re-run the linter to confirm all violations are resolved.
fix_strategies: 1. Run the linter to identify all import-related violations. 2. Remove any unused imports (imports present but not referenced in the file). 3. Move any imports that appear after executable code to the top of the file, before all other statements. 4. Re-run the linter to confirm all violations are resolved.
failure_reasons: Imports added but never used in the code (dead code)
Imports placed after variable assignments or other executable statements instead of at the module level

root_cause_pattern: Code was committed without being pre-formatted by the project's formatter (ruff-format), resulting in trailing whitespace, inconsistent indentation, and quote style violations that the pre-commit hook detects and rejects.
cascade_pattern: When a developer commits code that doesn't conform to formatting standards, the pre-commit hook runs the formatter which detects violations and exits with a non-zero code, blocking the commit and causing the CI pipeline to fail.
principle: Always run the project's code formatter (e.g., ruff-format, black, prettier) on changed files before committing. Formatters are designed to be run repeatedly and safely — they should be treated as a required step in the development workflow, not an optional cleanup task.
fix_strategy: 1. Run the project's formatter (ruff-format) on all changed files before committing. 2. Configure pre-commit hooks to auto-format on commit if supported. 3. Alternatively, use editor integrations to format on save. 4. Verify formatting passes locally by running the formatter and checking for changes before pushing.

root_cause_pattern: Using primitive or generic types (like `str`) instead of the specific enum or type provided by a third-party library for parameters that require precise type constraints. The developer used a loose type annotation that was functionally compatible at runtime but failed static type checking.
cascade_pattern: The type checker (pyright) validates parameter types against the library's type stubs and rejects the mismatched annotation. The failure is immediate and direct - the CI pipeline fails at the type-checking stage without proceeding to other checks.
principle: When integrating with third-party libraries, always use the specific types, enums, or type aliases that the library provides rather than primitive types. Library authors define these types to ensure type safety; using generic types defeats static type checking and causes CI failures. Always import and use the library's own type definitions for parameters that accept constrained values.
fix_strategy: 1. Identify the correct type from the third-party library's type stubs or documentation. 2. Add the necessary import for that type. 3. Replace the primitive/generic type annotation with the library's specific type. 4. Run the type checker to verify the fix resolves all related type mismatches.
fix_strategies: 1. Identify the correct type from the third-party library's type stubs or documentation. 2. Add the necessary import for that type. 3. Replace the primitive/generic type annotation with the library's specific type. 4. Run the type checker to verify the fix resolves all related type mismatches.
failure_patterns: Incorrect type annotation for library parameter
Primitive type used instead of library enum
failure_reasons: Type annotation used a generic `str` instead of the library-provided `ReasoningEffort` enum type
Static type checker enforced the library's type contract, rejecting the mismatched annotation

root_cause_pattern: Variable scope and initialization issues in conditional/branching code paths combined with type annotation mismatches — the fallback code path failed to initialize 'contents' before use, and type annotations did not match the actual types being passed to functions.
cascade_pattern: The unbound variable error (F823) triggered ruff to fail, which then exposed pyright type incompatibility issues, and finally ruff-format caught formatting inconsistencies — each tool caught a different layer of the same underlying problem stemming from variable handling in branching logic.
principle: When using conditional branches that return or assign values, always ensure every branch path explicitly initializes the variable before any reference. Use deep copies when modifying input data to prevent mutation side effects, and ensure type annotations precisely match the actual types being passed to prevent downstream type checking failures.
fix_strategy: 1. Audit all conditional branches for variable initialization before reference. 2. Ensure variables are defined in every code path (including else/fallback branches). 3. Use deep copies (model_copy(deep=True) or copy.deepcopy) when modifying input data. 4. Align type annotations with actual runtime types. 5. Run formatting checks to catch style inconsistencies that may mask logic errors.

Use deep copies (model_copy(deep=True) or copy.deepcopy) when modifying input data. 4. Align type annotations with actual runtime types. 5. Run formatting checks to catch style inconsistencies that may mask logic errors.

Type annotations specified 'str | PIL_Image | File | Part' but 'Content' type was being passed, causing pyright to reject the assignment

root_cause_pattern: A function's return type annotation was incomplete — it declared a narrower type (dict[str, type | None]) but the actual implementation could return additional types (UnionType objects) that were not included in the annotation. The developer added the UnionType to the code logic but failed to update both the import statement and the type annotation.
cascade_pattern: The static type checker (pyright) detects the mismatch between declared and actual return types at analysis time, causing the CI check to fail. If not caught, downstream code expecting only type | None would receive UnionType objects and could fail at runtime when attempting to use them as standard types.
principle: When implementing functions that can return multiple types, always ensure the return type annotation explicitly lists ALL possible types that could be returned. Any time you introduce a new return type in the implementation, you must also update the type annotation and ensure the type is imported. Static type checkers enforce strict type contracts and will reject code where the implementation returns types not covered by the annotation.
fix_strategy: 1. Identify all types returned by the function at runtime. 2. Ensure all returned types are imported. 3. Update the return type annotation to include all possible types using Union, |, or Any as appropriate. 4. Run the type checker to verify the fix resolves all type mismatches.
fix_strategies: 1. Identify all types returned by the function at runtime. 2. Ensure all returned types are imported. 3. Update the return type annotation to include all possible types using Union, |, or Any as appropriate. 4. Run the type checker to verify the fix resolves all type mismatches.
failure_reasons: Function return type annotation did not include all possible runtime return types
Developer added new return type to implementation but forgot to update type annotation and imports

principle: When debugging test failures, always consider that BOTH the implementation code AND the test code may contain bugs. Identify the expected format in test assertions. 4. Fix test delimiter or assertion logic to match actual output format. 5. Run tests to verify both fixes work together

root_cause_pattern: Tests contain hardcoded platform-specific path separators (e.g., Windows backslashes) in string assertions. When the CI environment runs on a different OS (e.g., Linux), the runtime path values use different separators (e.g., forward slashes), causing string comparison assertions to fail.
cascade_pattern: The test assertion compares a literal string with hardcoded separators against the actual runtime value. On a different platform, the runtime value uses its native separator, so the string mismatch causes the assertion to fail, blocking the CI pipeline.
principle: Always use platform-agnostic path construction methods (os.path.join, os.pathsep, pathlib.Path) when writing test assertions involving paths or path-like strings. Never hardcode separators like \ or / in test expectations — this ensures tests pass consistently across Windows, Linux, and macOS CI runners.
fix_strategy: 1. Identify all hardcoded path separators in test assertions. 2. Replace hardcoded separators with os.path.join(), os.pathsep, or pathlib.Path operations. 3. Use string formatting that abstracts the separator (e.g., f'path{os.sep}to{os.sep}file'). 4. Run tests on multiple platforms or enable cross-platform CI matrix testing to verify.

Use string formatting that abstracts the separator (e.g., f'path{os.sep}to{os.sep}file'). 4. Run tests on multiple platforms or enable cross-platform CI matrix testing to verify.

root_cause_pattern: Type validation logic uses strict type equality checks (type() comparison) instead of polymorphic type inspection (isinstance/issubclass), failing to recognize that different subtypes of a common abstract base type (e.g., int and float as subtypes of numbers.Number) are compatible.
cascade_pattern: When the composition function encounters values of different numeric subtypes, it performs type equality validation which rejects them despite both being numeric types, raising an exception that causes the test to fail and blocks the CI pipeline.
principle: When implementing value composition or merging logic for types that share a common abstract base class, always use polymorphic type checks (isinstance or issubclass) rather than strict type equality. This ensures different concrete implementations of a shared abstraction can be composed together. Specifically for numeric types in Python, leverage the numbers.Number abstract base class to recognize int, float, Decimal, and other numeric types as compatible.
fix_strategy: 1. Locate the type comparison logic causing the failure. 2. Replace direct type() equality checks with issubclass checks against the appropriate abstract base class (e.g., numbers.Number). 3. Add explicit conditional branches to skip type validation when both values are numeric subtypes. 4. Run composition tests with multiple numeric type combinations (int+float, int+Decimal, float+Decimal) to validate the fix.

Replace direct type() equality checks with issubclass checks against the appropriate abstract base class (e.g., numbers.Number). 3. Add explicit conditional branches to skip type validation when both values are numeric subtypes. 4. Run composition tests with multiple numeric type combinations (int+float, int+Decimal, float+Decimal) to validate the fix.
failure_reasons: Strict type equality validation rejects different numeric subtypes as incompatible
Code compares types using type() instead of leveraging abstract base classes like numbers.Number

root_cause_pattern: This class of failure stems from two contract mismatches: (1) shell command construction where variable interpolation is not protected against paths containing special characters, and (2) data structure contracts where the consumer assumes different key names than what the provider returns.
cascade_pattern: When shell variables contain spaces or special characters, the command fails to parse correctly, causing the git diff to abort. When dictionary keys mismatch between producer and consumer, the code raises a KeyError at runtime when attempting to access the non-existent keys, halting execution.
principle: Always validate and match the contract between data producers and consumers. For shell commands, quote all variable expansions to handle paths with spaces or special characters. For data structures, verify that key names used in code exactly match the keys returned by the underlying API or data source—never assume key names without confirming the actual contract.
fix_strategy: 1. Identify all shell commands that interpolate variables from external sources. 2. Add proper quoting (double quotes) around variable expansions to handle spaces and special characters. 3. Audit dictionary key access patterns to ensure they match the actual API response structure. 4. Use the exact key names returned by the provider (old_cache_path/new_cache_path) rather than assumed names. 5. Add defensive checks or use .get() methods to handle unexpected key variations.

Add proper quoting (double quotes) around variable expansions to handle spaces and special characters. 3. Audit dictionary key access patterns to ensure they match the actual API response structure. 4. Use the exact key names returned by the provider (old_cache_path/new_cache_path) rather than assumed names. 5. Add defensive checks or use .get() methods to handle unexpected key variations.
failure_reasons: Shell command constructed variables without quotes, causing failure when paths contain spaces
Code used dictionary keys that did not match the actual API response keys, causing KeyError at runtime

root_cause_pattern: Tests assert exact string output from external system tools (dpkg-query) without accounting for version-specific output format differences — the test expectations are tightly coupled to a specific version's output format rather than semantic results.
cascade_pattern: When the external tool's output format changes (due to OS version update like Ubuntu 24.04), the exact string match assertions fail first, causing the test suite to fail, which then blocks the CI pipeline from passing.
principle: When testing interactions with external system tools or dependencies, never assert on exact string output formats that may vary across versions. Instead, assert on semantic content (package presence/absence, exit codes, structured data) or use flexible matching patterns that tolerate minor format variations.
fix_strategy: 1. Identify tests asserting exact string output from external tools. 2. Refactor assertions to check semantic outcomes rather than exact text formats. 3. Use regex patterns, partial matching, or version-conditional expectations if format validation is necessary. 4. Prefer asserting on structured data or exit codes over raw text.

Use regex patterns, partial matching, or version-conditional expectations if format validation is necessary. 4. Prefer asserting on structured data or exit codes over raw text.
failure_reasons: Tests depend on exact string output format of external system tools that change between OS versions

root_cause_pattern: CI test infrastructure requires build tools (e.g., compilers, build systems) to be discoverable at test setup time. When the tool location configuration is incomplete or missing explicit paths for the CI platform, the test framework fails immediately during setup rather than gracefully handling the absence.
cascade_pattern: The test setup phase validates tool availability before any test code executes. If required tools are not found in the configured locations, the pytest_runtest_setup function invokes pytest.fail(), causing a cascading failure where zero tests run and the CI pipeline reports a complete test failure.
principle: Always explicitly configure tool paths in test infrastructure for each target CI platform, rather than relying on implicit PATH resolution. Test frameworks validate tool availability during setup, so any gap in tool configuration causes immediate setup-phase failure that blocks all downstream tests. Ensure the tools_locations or equivalent configuration maps each required tool to its platform-specific path on Linux, macOS, and Windows CI runners.
fix_strategy: 1. Identify all tools required by test infrastructure (check conftest.py or similar setup files). 2. Determine the installation paths for each tool on each CI platform (Linux, Darwin, Windows). 3. Add explicit path configurations to the tools_locations dictionary for all tools and platforms. 4. Verify the configuration passes test setup locally before pushing to CI.

Determine the installation paths for each tool on each CI platform (Linux, Darwin, Windows). 3. Add explicit path configurations to the tools_locations dictionary for all tools and platforms. 4. Verify the configuration passes test setup locally before pushing to CI.

root_cause_pattern: A variable is assigned a value but never referenced or used in subsequent code, triggering linter rules designed to catch dead or unnecessary code. This pattern occurs when developers write function calls for side effects but accidentally capture the return value in a variable.
cascade_pattern: The linter scans the code and detects the unused variable assignment, exiting with a non-zero status code. This causes the CI lint job to fail, blocking the pipeline from proceeding.
principle: Always ensure that variable assignments serve a purpose — if you need the return value, use it; if you only need the side effects, call the function without assignment. Linters are configured to catch these patterns because unused variables indicate bugs, incomplete refactoring, or dead code.
fix_strategy: 1. Identify the unused variable assignment in the linter error message. 2. Determine whether the return value is needed — if yes, use the variable; if no, remove the assignment and call the function standalone. 3. Run the linter again to verify the fix passes. 4. Confirm CI lint job succeeds.
fix_strategies: 1. Identify the unused variable assignment in the linter error message. 2. Determine whether the return value is needed — if yes, use the variable; if no, remove the assignment and call the function standalone. 3. Run the linter again to verify the fix passes. 4. Confirm CI lint job succeeds.
failure_reasons: A local variable was assigned the result of a function call but never used in the code
The ruff linter detected the F841 violation and exited with code 1, failing the CI job

root_cause_pattern: The failure stems from incorrect message role semantics (using 'assistant' role for system-level prompts instead of 'system' role) combined with missing state tracking for tool actions in stream processing components, and redundant method calls causing inefficient execution.
cascade_pattern: When a system prompt uses an incorrect role, downstream message handling fails validation. When tool action tracking is missing, downstream functions receive unexpected keyword arguments causing test failures. principle: Always use the semantically correct role for each message type in LLM service code—system prompts must use the 'system' role, not 'assistant'. Avoid redundant method calls by caching results when the same computation is needed multiple times within a single execution path.

Identify all message construction points and verify each uses the correct role for its purpose (system prompts use 'system', user prompts use 'user', assistant responses use 'assistant'). 2. Add instance variable state tracking for any tool actions or parameters needed by downstream components. 3. Cache method results that are computed multiple times in the same execution path. 4. Run tests to verify the fixes resolve all downstream failures.

root_cause_pattern: Tests become misaligned with implementation changes (stale assertions) and mock fixtures fail to properly isolate test context by not cleaning sys.modules, allowing real modules to leak into the test environment.
cascade_pattern: Stale assertions cause immediate test failures when implementation behavior changes; sys.modules contamination causes real modules to load instead of mocks, leading to downstream errors like authentication failures that mask the actual isolation problem.
principle: Test assertions must remain synchronized with implementation behavior — whenever implementation changes, corresponding test assertions must be updated. Additionally, mock fixtures must properly clean up sys.modules before and after patching to guarantee true isolation from real modules, preventing real module contamination that causes cryptic downstream failures.
fix_strategy: 1. Audit test assertions to verify they match actual implementation behavior. 2. Ensure mock fixtures clean up sys.modules entries for the mocked module and its submodules before and after patching. 3. Run tests in isolated environments to verify no real module leakage occurs. 4. Update test expectations immediately when implementation behavior changes.
fix_strategies: 1. Audit test assertions to verify they match actual implementation behavior. 2. Ensure mock fixtures clean up sys.modules entries for the mocked module and its submodules before and after patching. 3. Run tests in isolated environments to verify no real module leakage occurs. 4. Update test expectations immediately when implementation behavior changes.

Mock fixture not properly cleaning sys.modules allowing real module contamination

root_cause_pattern: Python source files not conforming to PEP 8 formatting standards — specifically missing a required blank line after module-level docstrings and missing trailing newlines at end of file. These are whitespace/formatting violations that linting tools enforce.
cascade_pattern: When formatting violations exist in Python files, pre-commit hooks designed to catch style issues will fail. In this case, the CI pipeline failed earlier at dependency installation (uv), but the underlying formatting issues would have caused pre-commit failure if the workflow had progressed further.
principle: Always ensure Python files conform to PEP 8 formatting standards before committing. The two critical formatting requirements that frequently cause CI failures are: (1) a blank line must follow module-level docstrings, and (2) files must end with a trailing newline. These are enforced by pre-commit hooks and constitute basic Python style compliance.
fix_strategy: 1. Add a blank line after every module-level docstring in Python files. 2. Ensure every Python file ends with a trailing newline character. 3. Run pre-commit hooks locally before pushing to catch formatting issues early. 4. Configure editors to automatically insert trailing newlines and validate PEP 8 compliance.
fix_strategies: 1. Add a blank line after every module-level docstring in Python files. 2. Ensure every Python file ends with a trailing newline character. 3. Run pre-commit hooks locally before pushing to catch formatting issues early. 4. Configure editors to automatically insert trailing newlines and validate PEP 8 compliance.
failure_reasons: Python files missing required PEP 8 whitespace formatting after docstrings
Python files not terminated with a newline character, violating PEP 8 end-of-file requirements

root_cause_pattern: Documentation and tests were written based on an incorrect or outdated specification reference (RFC 2045) that did not match the actual implementation behavior governed by a newer/correct specification (RFC 9110), causing both documentation build and test execution to fail when they encountered the mismatch.
cascade_pattern: The implementation correctly returned 'application/octet-stream' for invalid Content-Type headers per RFC 9110. This triggered parallel failures: the documentation build failed because it incorrectly documented 'text/plain' per RFC 2045, and the test failed because it asserted 'text/plain' instead of 'application/octet-stream'. Both failures are independent symptoms of the same underlying misre...
principle: When documenting or testing behavior that depends on external specifications (such as RFCs), always verify that the documentation and test assertions match what the implementation actually does—not what an older or different specification states. Mismatches between documented/expected behavior and actual implementation will cause both documentation builds and tests to fail.
fix_strategy: 1. Verify the actual implementation behavior against the correct specification. 2. Update test assertions to match the implementation behavior. 3. Update documentation to accurately describe the implementation behavior with the correct specification reference. 4. Run both tests and documentation builds to confirm consistency.
fix_strategies: 1. Verify the actual implementation behavior against the correct specification. 2. Update test assertions to match the implementation behavior. 3. Update documentation to accurately describe the implementation behavior with the correct specification reference. 4. Run both tests and documentation builds to confirm consistency.

Test assertion expected behavior (text/plain) that did not match implementation behavior (application/octet-stream)

root_cause_pattern: CI validation tooling (slotscheck, spell checker) enforces strict structural and documentation rules that are not automatically updated when code or documentation changes — missing slot definitions or unrecognized words cause build failures regardless of functional correctness.
cascade_pattern: When developers modify code or documentation without updating corresponding validation artifacts (slot definitions, wordlists), the CI pipeline fails at validation steps before or alongside functional tests, blocking merge even though the core changes are correct.
principle: CI validation tools maintain their own state (whitelists, slot definitions, configuration) that must be explicitly updated alongside code and documentation changes. Treat validation configuration as a first-class artifact that requires synchronization with functional changes — never assume documentation words or class definitions are automatically recognized by CI tooling.
fix_strategy: 1. Identify which CI validation tool failed (slotscheck, sphinx spell checker, etc.). 2. Locate the corresponding configuration or whitelist file (wordlist.txt, slot definitions). 3. Add the missing entry (word, __slots__ definition) to satisfy the validation requirement. 4. Verify the fix passes CI before merging.
fix_strategies: 1. Identify which CI validation tool failed (slotscheck, sphinx spell checker, etc.). 2. Locate the corresponding configuration or whitelist file (wordlist.txt, slot definitions). 3. Add the missing entry (word, __slots__ definition) to satisfy the validation requirement. 4. Verify the fix passes CI before merging.
failure_reasons: Class slot definitions not declared or updated when class structure changed, triggering slotscheck validation failure
Documentation term used in code or docs was not pre-approved in the CI spell-check whitelist, causing validation failure

root_cause_pattern: Using incorrect string identifiers (import paths or model strings) that do not match the actual module/service implementation — the strings reference non-existent modules or use incompatible format specifiers that the system cannot resolve.
cascade_pattern: An incorrect import path causes ModuleNotFoundError during pytest test collection, which halts the entire test suite before any tests run. This early-stage failure prevents downstream test failures from being discovered or executed, masking independent issues.
principle: When referencing external modules, classes, or service identifiers in code and tests, always use the exact fully-qualified string format that matches the actual implementation. Incorrect string identifiers cause immediate failures during test collection or initialization, preventing the test suite from running and masking other independent failures.
fix_strategy: 1. Verify the correct import path or identifier format from the actual module/service implementation. 2. Use fully-qualified paths (e.g., 'module.submodule.class') rather than abbreviated or assumed paths. 3. For service/model identifiers, use the provider-prefixed format (e.g., 'provider/model-name') as required by the implementation. 4. Run test collection separately to ensure imports resolve before running tests.
fix_strategies: 1. Verify the correct import path or identifier format from the actual module/service implementation. 2. Use fully-qualified paths (e.g., 'module.submodule.class') rather than abbreviated or assumed paths. 3. For service/model identifiers, use the provider-prefixed format (e.g., 'provider/model-name') as required by the implementation. 4. Run test collection separately to ensure imports resolve before running tests.

Test uses bare model identifier that the LLM implementation cannot resolve to a valid provider/model combination

root_cause_pattern: Code containing linting violations (unused imports, bare except clauses, unused variables) was committed to the repository. The CI pipeline runs ruff check which detects these violations and returns a non-zero exit code, causing the lint job to fail.
cascade_pattern: When ruff detects violations, it exits with a non-zero code. This causes the CI workflow's lint step to fail, which blocks the entire CI pipeline and prevents the commit from being merged.
principle: Always run linting tools locally before pushing code to CI. Unused imports and bare except clauses are code quality issues that violate linting standards — remove unused imports, replace bare except with specific exception handling, and either use or remove unused variables to ensure code passes all lint checks.
fix_strategy: 1. Run the linter locally (e.g., ruff check) before pushing. 2. Remove all unused imports (F401). 3. Replace bare except clauses with specific exception types (E722). 4. Either use or remove unused variables (F841). 5. Re-run the linter to verify all violations are resolved. 6. Commit the fixed code and push.
fix_strategies: 1. Run the linter locally (e.g., ruff check) before pushing. 2. Remove all unused imports (F401). 3. Replace bare except clauses with specific exception types (E722). 4. Either use or remove unused variables (F841). 5. Re-run the linter to verify all violations are resolved. 6. Commit the fixed code and push.
failure_reasons: Code contains imports that are imported but never used in the file (F401)
Code uses bare except clauses that catch all exceptions including system-exiting exceptions (E722)

root_cause_pattern: Import ordering in a module creates an incorrect type resolution chain that corrupts type information mypy uses when analyzing downstream modules that depend on types from that module.
cascade_pattern: When a module has incorrect import ordering, mypy's type inference in downstream modules fails with seemingly unrelated type errors (incompatible arguments, assignment mismatches, non-indexable types) because the type resolution chain established during import processing is broken or incorrect.
principle: The order of imports in a Python module affects how mypy resolves and propagates type information to dependent modules. Incorrect import ordering can create a corrupted type resolution chain that causes type inference failures in downstream modules that have no direct code issues. Always ensure imports are ordered correctly (standard library → third-party → local) to establish a valid type resolution order.
fix_strategy: 1. Identify downstream files with type errors that share module dependencies. 2. Examine import ordering in the source module that provides types to those downstream files. 3. Reorder imports to follow standard Python convention (stdlib → third-party → local). 4. Run mypy to verify type errors in downstream files are resolved. 5. If errors persist, check for circular dependencies or missing type annotations that may also affect resolution.
fix_strategies: 1. Identify downstream files with type errors that share module dependencies. 2. Examine import ordering in the source module that provides types to those downstream files. 3. Reorder imports to follow standard Python convention (stdlib → third-party → local). 4. Run mypy to verify type errors in downstream files are resolved. 5. If errors persist, check for circular dependencies or missing type annotations that may also affect resolution.
failure_reasons: Incorrect import ordering in a module creates an invalid type resolution chain that causes mypy to fail type inference in downstream dependent modules
Import order causing mypy type resolution failure leading to cascading type errors in unrelated downstream files

root_cause_pattern: Static type checking (mypy) failures occur when type annotations are missing, incorrect, or inconsistent in source code. This typically happens when code changes introduce new functions, parameters, or return values without corresponding type hints, or when type annotations become stale after refactoring.
cascade_pattern: When the type-checking job fails, it blocks the entire linter job from completing successfully. Since CI pipelines typically require all jobs in a stage to pass before proceeding, downstream test jobs cannot execute, preventing verification of code correctness.
principle: Static type checking is a gatekeeping mechanism in CI pipelines — type errors are not warnings but blocking failures that halt the entire pipeline. Developers must treat type annotations as first-class code artifacts that require the same rigor as the code itself. Running type checkers locally before committing is essential to prevent pipeline blockages that cascade to downstream test execution.
fix_strategy: 1. Run mypy or equivalent type checker locally before committing. 2. Address all reported type errors systematically (missing return types, incorrect annotations, untyped dependencies). 3. Verify type consistency across module boundaries. 4. Re-run type checker to confirm all errors are resolved. 5. Ensure CI type checking passes before considering the fix complete.

Address all reported type errors systematically (missing return types, incorrect annotations, untyped dependencies). 3. Verify type consistency across module boundaries. 4. Re-run type checker to confirm all errors are resolved. 5. Ensure CI type checking passes before considering the fix complete.

Type errors in source files prevented the CI pipeline from proceeding to downstream test execution

principle: Automated spelling and typo detection tools in CI pipelines will catch any misspelled words in source code. Developers must run these tools locally before pushing code to ensure all spelling errors are corrected, as even minor typos in identifiers or comments will cause CI failures.
fix_strategy: 1. Run the typos/spell-check CI tool locally before committing. 2. Fix any spelling errors identified by the tool. 3. Re-run the tool to verify all errors are resolved. 4. Commit the corrected code.
