Incorrect spelling of a common term (Hitable instead of Hittable) in code identifiers

root_cause_pattern: A CI linter (typos tool) detected errors in one language's files (TypeScript), but the ground-truth fix modified files in a different language (Python) that did not contain the detected errors, indicating a mismatch between what the CI tool flagged and what was actually fixed.
cascade_pattern: When CI detects errors in specific files but fixes are applied to unrelated files, the root cause remains unfixed while secondary issues get addressed, leading to potential re-failures and confusion about what the actual problem was.
principle: When a CI tool reports a specific failure, the fix must address the exact files and issues the tool flagged. Blindly modifying files in the same commit without verifying they contain the reported errors wastes CI cycles and leaves the original problem unresolved. Always verify that your changes actually address what the CI tool complained about.
fix_strategy: 1. Identify the exact files and line numbers reported by the failing CI tool. 2. Verify the reported errors exist in those specific files. 3. Apply fixes only to the files containing the actual errors. 4. Re-run CI to confirm the specific failure is resolved. 5. Address any additional issues found in those same files in the same commit.
fix_strategies: 1. Identify the exact files and line numbers reported by the failing CI tool. 2. Verify the reported errors exist in those specific files. 3. Apply fixes only to the files containing the actual errors. 4. Re-run CI to confirm the specific failure is resolved. 5. Address any additional issues found in those same files in the same commit.
failure_reasons: CI tool detected errors in TypeScript files but fixes were applied to Python files that did not contain those errors
Developer applied changes to unrelated files in the same commit without verifying they contained the CI-flagged issues

root_cause_pattern: Code passes a potentially None-valued optional parameter directly to a constructor or function that requires a non-null type (e.g., Path()) without first validating the parameter is not None, causing a TypeError at initialization time.
cascade_pattern: The TypeError occurs during object initialization before any tests run, causing the entire test suite to fail because the class cannot be instantiated. This masks any actual test failures and blocks the CI pipeline.
principle: When handling optional parameters that may be None, always perform defensive null checks BEFORE passing them to constructors or functions that expect non-null types. This applies especially in __init__ methods where failures prevent the entire object from being created, cascading into mass test failures.
fix_strategy: 1. Identify all optional parameters with default values of None. 2. Add explicit null checks before using them in operations requiring non-null types. 3. Use conditional initialization patterns (if param is not None: ...). 4. Ensure proper default handling or early return when null values are encountered. 5. Validate null handling covers all code paths in initialization.
fix_strategies: 1. Identify all optional parameters with default values of None. 2. Add explicit null checks before using them in operations requiring non-null types. 3. Use conditional initialization patterns (if param is not None: ...). 4. Ensure proper default handling or early return when null values are encountered. 5. Validate null handling covers all code paths in initialization.
failure_reasons: Optional parameter defaulted to None was passed directly to Path() constructor without null check
Code assumed optional parameter would always have a valid value during object initialization

root_cause_pattern: A unit or scale mismatch exists between the hardcoded expected values in test assertions and the actual unit format returned by an external data source or cache. Tests assume one measurement scale (e.g., per token) while the data source uses a different scale (e.g., per million tokens).
cascade_pattern: When the test runs, the assertion compares actual values in the source's native unit against expected values in a different unit. The comparison fails because the numeric values differ by orders of magnitude, causing the test to fail even though the underlying data is correct.
principle: Always verify and align the unit of measurement between your test expectations and the external data source. When testing code that retrieves cached or API-sourced data, confirm whether the values are in per-unit, per-thousand, or per-million format. Hardcode expected test values that match the actual unit the source provides, or implement explicit unit conversion in the data layer.
fix_strategy: 1. Identify the actual unit format used by the external data source or cache. 2. Update test assertion expected values to match the source's native unit. 3. If a different unit is desired in the output, add explicit unit conversion logic in the application code rather than relying on test-time adjustments. 4. Document the expected unit format in the test to prevent future confusion.
fix_strategies: 1. Identify the actual unit format used by the external data source or cache. 2. Update test assertion expected values to match the source's native unit. 3. If a different unit is desired in the output, add explicit unit conversion logic in the application code rather than relying on test-time adjustments. 4. Document the expected unit format in the test to prevent future confusion.
failure_reasons: Test assertions used values in 'dollars per token' but the OpenRouter cache stores values in 'dollars per million tokens', causing a 1000000x numerical difference
Hardcoded test expectations did not match the actual measurement unit returned by the external service

root_cause_pattern: Code was written in a style that does not conform to the project's formatter (black) rules, causing the formatter to want to reformat it. The CI/pre-commit hook is configured to fail when the formatter makes ANY modifications, treating unformatted code as a failure.
cascade_pattern: When the formatter runs in CI, it detects formatting differences between the current code and its own style guide. It modifies the file to conform, but the CI interprets these modifications as a failure (exit code 1), even though the code is functionally correct. This blocks the build until the formatter's changes are accepted.
principle: Always run formatters locally before pushing code. CI formatter checks are designed to enforce consistent style, not to apply fixes—they expect code to already be formatted. When a formatter detects differences and wants to reformat, the correct response is to accept those changes locally, not to treat them as a CI bug. Formatters like black are idempotent: running them again produces stable output.
fix_strategy: 1. Run the formatter (e.g., black) locally on the affected file(s). 2. Review the formatter's changes to confirm they are correct style adjustments. 3. Stage the formatted files and commit them. 4. Push to trigger CI again, which should now pass.
fix_strategies: 1. Run the formatter (e.g., black) locally on the affected file(s). 2. Review the formatter's changes to confirm they are correct style adjustments. 3. Stage the formatted files and commit them. 4. Push to trigger CI again, which should now pass.
failure_reasons: Code written across multiple lines that the formatter collapses to a single line, triggering a reformat failure
CI/pre-commit configured to fail when formatter makes any file modifications, treating unformatted code as a build failure

root_cause_pattern: Importing an entire module (e.g., `import copy`) while only using a specific function from it (e.g., `deepcopy`) triggers an F401 'imported but unused' error in flake8. The linter detects that the module-level import is unused because the code only references the specific function without the module prefix.
cascade_pattern: The flake8 F401 error causes the linting check to fail with exit code 1, which causes pre-commit hooks to fail, which causes the CI workflow to fail. The failure propagates upward from the static analysis tool through the CI infrastructure.
principle: Always use the most specific import form that matches your usage pattern: import specific functions directly (`from module import function`) rather than importing the whole module when you only need one item. This allows static analysis tools to properly track import usage and prevents false-positive F401 errors. Run linting tools locally before pushing to catch these issues early.
fix_strategy: 1. Run the linting tool locally (e.g., flake8) to identify F401 errors. 2. Identify which specific functions from the imported module are actually used in the file. 3. Change the import statement from `import module` to `from module import specific_function`. 4. Update any references to use the direct function name instead of module.function. 5. Re-run the linting tool to verify the fix resolves all F401 errors.
fix_strategies: 1. Run the linting tool locally (e.g., flake8) to identify F401 errors. 2. Identify which specific functions from the imported module are actually used in the file. 3. Change the import statement from `import module` to `from module import specific_function`. 4. Update any references to use the direct function name instead of module.function. 5. Re-run the linting tool to verify the fix resolves all F401 errors.
failure_reasons: Importing an entire module while only using a specific function triggers F401 'imported but unused' in flake8
The static analysis tool fails on unused imports, causing pre-commit and CI pipelines to fail

root_cause_pattern: A subclass method override does not include all parameters defined in the parent class method signature, creating an incompatible interface that violates the Liskov Substitution Principle — the subclass cannot be used as a drop-in replacement for the parent because it accepts fewer arguments.
cascade_pattern: When the type checker (mypy) analyzes the inheritance hierarchy, it detects that the subclass method signature is not a valid override of the parent method. The type checker fails because the contract of the parent class is not being honored by the subclass, breaking type safety and substitutability.
principle: When overriding methods in an object-oriented language, the subclass method signature must be compatible with the parent class signature — it must accept all parameters the parent accepts (or more). This is the Liskov Substitution Principle: objects of a superclass shall be replaceable with objects of a subclass without affecting correctness. Always use a type checker like mypy to catch signature mismatches in inheritance hierarchies.
fix_strategy: 1. Identify the parent class method signature and all its parameters. 2. Add any missing parameters to the subclass override method signature. 3. Provide sensible default values for new parameters to maintain backward compatibility. 4. Update the method body to use the new parameters appropriately. 5. Run the type checker to verify the fix resolves all signature incompatibility errors.
fix_strategies: 1. Identify the parent class method signature and all its parameters. 2. Add any missing parameters to the subclass override method signature. 3. Provide sensible default values for new parameters to maintain backward compatibility. 4. Update the method body to use the new parameters appropriately. 5. Run the type checker to verify the fix resolves all signature incompatibility errors.
failure_reasons: Subclass method override missing parameters that exist in parent class method signature
Type checker detects incompatible method signatures that violate the Liskov Substitution Principle

root_cause_pattern: The dependency lock file was not regenerated after the dependency specification file was modified, causing a version and content-hash mismatch between the two files that the dependency manager detects and refuses to proceed with.
cascade_pattern: When the CI pipeline attempts to install dependencies, the dependency manager detects the lock file inconsistency and halts the installation process, blocking all subsequent CI steps that depend on the installed environment.
principle: Always regenerate lock files immediately after modifying dependency specification files, and commit both files together. Lock files exist to ensure reproducible builds; their purpose is defeated when they become stale. Treat lock file updates as an atomic part of any dependency change.
fix_strategy: 1. After modifying pyproject.toml (or equivalent dependency spec), run the lock file regeneration command (e.g., 'poetry lock'). 2. Verify the lock file is regenerated and includes the expected changes. 3. Commit both the dependency specification file and the regenerated lock file together in the same commit. 4. In CI, consider adding a pre-install check (e.g., 'poetry lock --check') to catch desynchronization early.
fix_strategies: 1. After modifying pyproject.toml (or equivalent dependency spec), run the lock file regeneration command (e.g., 'poetry lock'). 2. Verify the lock file is regenerated and includes the expected changes. 3. Commit both the dependency specification file and the regenerated lock file together in the same commit. 4. In CI, consider adding a pre-install check (e.g., 'poetry lock --check') to catch desynchronization early.
failure_reasons: Lock file not regenerated after dependency specification changes
Version constraint mismatch between dependency specification file and lock file
Content-hash mismatch indicating lock file staleness

root_cause_pattern: A class lacks a proper __init__ method, forcing initialization logic to be performed inline in methods, which creates unused variable assignments that trigger lint warnings.
cascade_pattern: Fixing a structural code issue (adding __init__ method) requires updating corresponding test files. When test updates are made without running formatters, they introduce formatting violations that cause separate CI failures in subsequent steps.
principle: When refactoring class structure to fix lint warnings, always run formatters on both production code AND any modified test files before committing. A fix in one file can cascade into formatting violations in dependent files, causing CI to fail at a different step than the original issue.
fix_strategy: 1. Fix the root cause by adding proper __init__ method to handle initialization. 2. Update all test files that instantiate or test the modified class. 3. Run formatters (Black) on all modified files including tests. 4. Run full CI pipeline to verify no downstream failures.
fix_strategies: 1. Fix the root cause by adding proper __init__ method to handle initialization. 2. Update all test files that instantiate or test the modified class. 3. Run formatters (Black) on all modified files including tests. 4. Run full CI pipeline to verify no downstream failures.
failure_reasons: Class lacks __init__ method, causing initialization logic to be placed inline in methods with unused variable assignments
Test file modifications made without running formatters introduce inconsistent indentation and formatting violations

root_cause_pattern: When developers add new imports to a file, they often neglect to place them in the correct alphabetical order required by the project's import sorting tool configuration, causing the CI formatting check to fail.
cascade_pattern: The CI pipeline runs automated formatting checks (isort) before allowing merges. When imports are not sorted correctly according to the tool's configuration, the format check fails with a non-zero exit code, blocking the build and preventing the code change from being merged.
principle: Always ensure that any new imports are placed in the correct alphabetical order as defined by the project's isort configuration. Run local formatting checks (isort and full format validation) before pushing code to catch import sorting violations early and avoid CI pipeline failures.
fix_strategy: 1. When adding new imports, immediately place them in the correct alphabetical order relative to existing imports. 2. Run the import sorting tool (isort) locally on modified files before committing. 3. Run the full CI format check command locally (e.g., tox -e format_check) to validate all formatting rules pass before pushing.

root_cause_pattern: A developer confused set literal syntax with dict literal syntax when passing a dictionary value to a parameter that expects a mapping type. In Python, `{"key", value}` creates a set containing a string and a dict (which is unhashable), while `{"key": value}` creates a dict with key-value pairs.
cascade_pattern: When Python attempts to add an unhashable dict to a set, it raises a TypeError at the point of set creation. This causes the test to fail immediately, preventing any further test execution for that particular test case.
principle: When providing dictionary values to parameters that expect mapping types (such as extensions, headers, or kwargs), always use dict literal syntax with colons (`key: value`) rather than set literal syntax with commas (`key, value`). The colon is the distinguishing character that tells Python you intend a dict, not a set. This mistake is especially insidious because the syntax looks similar but has fundamentally different runtime behavior.
fix_strategy: 1. Identify parameters expecting dict/mapping types in function signatures. 2. When passing literal values, verify dict syntax uses colons (`:`) for key-value pairs, not commas (`,`). 3. For empty dict values, use `{"key": {}}` not `{"key", {}}`. 4. Run static type checkers or linters that can catch unhashable type errors before runtime. 5. Add test cases that verify extension/header parameters accept valid dict structures.

When passing literal values, verify dict syntax uses colons (`:`) for key-value pairs, not commas (`,`). 3. For empty dict values, use `{"key": {}}` not `{"key", {}}`. 4. Run static type checkers or linters that can catch unhashable type errors before runtime. 5. Add test cases that verify extension/header parameters accept valid dict structures.

When a failure matches known infrastructure issues (missing templates, 500 errors), diagnose the build pipeline rather than the code diff.

root_cause_pattern: When developers add new CLI arguments or configuration attributes to production code, they often implement the production code change but fail to update related test fixtures to include the new attributes, and may also introduce formatting violations in the new code.
cascade_pattern: The new production code triggers two parallel failures: (1) style checkers flag formatting violations in the newly added code, and (2) tests fail because test fixtures lack the attributes that production code now expects to access, causing AttributeError at runtime.
principle: When adding new arguments, attributes, or configuration options to production code, developers must proactively update BOTH the code formatting AND all test fixtures/mocks to include the new attributes. Incomplete feature implementation—where production code is updated but supporting test infrastructure is not—will cause CI failures across multiple check types.
fix_strategy: 1. Run formatting tools (Black, isort, etc.) and apply auto-fixes to new code. 2. Audit all test fixtures and mock classes to identify which ones need new attributes. 3. Add the missing attributes to fixtures with appropriate default values. 4. Re-run full test suite to verify all fixtures are complete.

root_cause_pattern: Auto-generated or continuously-extended source files (such as protocol bindings, dissector tables, or large constant definitions) exceed the configured maximum line length as they grow over time, triggering the E501 line-length lint rule.
cascade_pattern: When a source file contains a line that exceeds the configured character limit, the flake8 linter emits E501 and exits with a non-zero status, causing the CI lint job to fail; documentation warnings treated as errors can compound the failure.
principle: Any codebase that uses code generators, auto-generated protocol bindings, or large constant tables must ensure the generation layer respects the project's configured line-length limit, or the linting configuration must explicitly allow an acceptable greater limit. Long lines should be shortened via logical splitting, intermediate variables, or continuation lines rather than leaving them to exceed the enforced constraint.
fix_strategy: 1. Identify the file and line causing the E501 violation. 2. Determine whether the content can be shortened (split across lines, use variables, refactor). 3. If the content legitimately requires more characters, raise the allowed limit in the linting configuration to a pragmatic value. 4. If using a code generator, update the generator to respect the line-length constraint. 5. Verify the fix passes lint before pushing.

root_cause_pattern: Code changes introduced formatting violations (trailing whitespace, missing trailing newlines at end of files, or lines exceeding maximum length) that were not detected or fixed before the code was committed and pushed to the repository.
cascade_pattern: When CI runs pre-commit hooks on the submitted code, the formatting checks detect these violations and fail with exit code 1, blocking the CI pipeline from completing. The failure is immediate and prevents any downstream tests or jobs from running.
principle: Always run the same linting and formatting checks locally that your CI pipeline will run, before pushing code. Configure pre-commit hooks to run automatically on every commit to catch formatting issues early. This ensures code meets style standards before it reaches CI, preventing build failures caused by trivial formatting discrepancies.
fix_strategy: 1. Run pre-commit hooks locally (pre-commit run --all-files) before pushing. 2. Fix each formatting violation: remove trailing whitespace, add trailing newlines to files ending without them, and reformat long lines to comply with line-length limits. 3. Re-run pre-commit hooks to verify all issues are resolved. 4. Commit the formatting fixes and push.
